raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable-device therapy for selected patients with symptomatic heart failure (HF), designed to augment myocardial performance without initiating a propagated action potential. Contemporary HF care is anchored in disease-modifying pharmacotherapy and device therapy, yet many patients remain limited by exertional symptoms despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [1,2]. Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibition and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibition have reduced morbidity and mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [3-5]. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) improve outcomes in appropriately selected patients, especially those with electrical dyssynchrony, but CRT benefit is attenuated when QRS duration is narrow or mechanical dyssynchrony is absent [6-9]. CCM was developed to address this residual therapeutic gap.

CCM delivers relatively high-voltage biphasic electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, typically for several hours daily. Because the stimulus is timed after depolarization, it does not trigger a new contraction; rather, it appears to modulate intracellular calcium handling, myofilament responsiveness, autonomic tone, and myocardial gene expression [10-12]. Early human and animal studies showed acute improvements in contractility without increased myocardial oxygen consumption of the magnitude expected from catecholaminergic inotropy [10-13]. This distinction is central: CCM is best conceptualized as electrical modulation of failing myocardium, not chronic pacing and not pharmacologic inotropic support.

Mechanistic investigations have reported normalization of fetal-gene-expression patterns, improved sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase expression, reduced maladaptive neurohormonal signaling, and favorable effects on ventricular remodeling [14-16]. In myocardial biopsy studies from patients receiving CCM, expression of genes involved in calcium cycling and contractile function shifted toward non-failing profiles [16]. These findings support the hypothesis that CCM has biological effects extending beyond immediate hemodynamic augmentation.

Clinical evaluation has proceeded through feasibility studies, randomized trials, post-market registries, and meta-analyses. Early studies established implant feasibility and suggested improvements in New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, peak oxygen consumption, and quality of life in patients with advanced HF and narrow QRS complexes [17]. The FIX-HF-4 and FIX-HF-5 programs provided the main randomized evidence base. In FIX-HF-5, CCM did not meet its primary ventilatory anaerobic threshold endpoint in the overall cohort but improved several patient-centered measures, including Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire score and peak oxygen consumption in prespecified subgroups [18]. Subsequent enrichment strategies focused on patients with NYHA class III symptoms, sinus rhythm, QRS duration not meeting CRT criteria, and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) generally between 25% and 45%. FIX-HF-5C demonstrated improved exercise capacity and health status with acceptable safety, contributing to regulatory adoption in selected patients [19]. A later two-lead system study supported simplification of implantation while preserving performance and safety [20].

Meta-analyses generally show that CCM improves functional capacity, NYHA class, and quality of life, while evidence for mortality and HF hospitalization reduction remains less definitive because trials have been relatively small and not primarily powered for hard clinical outcomes [21,22]. Observational registries and longer-term follow-up series have suggested durable symptomatic improvement and potentially lower-than-predicted mortality in real-world populations, but these findings are vulnerable to selection bias and confounding [23-26]. CCM has also been explored in patients who are CRT nonresponders or not candidates for CRT, reflecting its mechanistic independence from electrical resynchronization [27].

Patient selection is therefore crucial. The most evidence-supported candidates are patients with persistent NYHA class III symptoms despite GDMT, LVEF in the moderately reduced HFrEF range, narrow QRS complexes or no CRT indication, and absence of frequent ventricular ectopy or atrial arrhythmias that prevent reliable signal delivery. CCM is not a substitute for GDMT, ICD therapy when indicated, CRT when indicated, revascularization, valve intervention, or advanced HF therapies. It should be considered only after optimization of medical therapy and reassessment of congestion, ischemia, rhythm status, mitral regurgitation, renal function, iron deficiency, sleep-disordered breathing, and adherence.

Safety considerations include standard device-related risks: pocket hematoma, infection, lead dislodgement, venous obstruction, tricuspid valve interaction, and device-device interactions in patients with ICDs. Modern systems are designed for compatibility with defibrillators, but careful sensing assessment and follow-up are required. Unlike CRT, CCM does not depend on left ventricular coronary sinus lead placement, which may simplify implantation in some patients. However, the therapy requires procedural expertise, programming follow-up, and realistic counseling: symptomatic and exercise gains are more established than survival benefit.

Important unanswered questions remain. Trials powered for HF hospitalization and mortality are needed, particularly in the era of quadruple GDMT. The optimal LVEF range, benefit in atrial fibrillation, interaction with ICD and CRT systems, cost-effectiveness, and biological predictors of response require further study [28-30]. In summary, CCM is a mechanistically distinctive, symptom-focused device therapy for carefully selected patients with persistent HF symptoms who lack a CRT indication. Its current role is adjunctive: it may improve functional capacity and quality of life, but it should be deployed within comprehensive HF programs that emphasize GDMT optimization, shared decision-making, and longitudinal outcome assessment.
